newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Gold - Far East dealers see slow weeks ahead.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold - Far East dealers see slow weeks ahead.

text.p: Far East gold traders are looking ahead to another lacklustre week as they wait to see where the money that took flight from international equities markets comes to rest.
"There is still a negative attitude towards the metals," an analyst with an international trading house in Hong Kong said.

Asian gold prices would probably be locked in range-trading over the next week, dealers in Hong Kong and Singapore said. Most polled by Reuters saw some consolidation, with physical demand seen remaining steady if unspectacular.
"Gold is just consolidating around US$366 to $371 an ounce," a trader for a Singapore-based bank said. "The steady physical demand is enabling the market to hold a bit at these levels."
"I don't think gold will move very much. It will stay here for a quite a while," another dealer said.
"It's depressing," he said.

Traders said the market was still reeling from a shift in funds to Wall Street and other stock markets like Hong Kong's. Even though the Dow fell by 70 points on Wednesday, the slide barely affected Asian gold prices, Singapore sources said.
"The market came down and gold barely moved," one dealer said. "People are just not interested in gold at the moment."
Singapore gold premiums were quoted slightly easier at around 35-45 U.S. cents an ounce over spot London prices mainly because of slack demand, dealers said.
A Singapore-based jeweller said the weakness of gold was being compounded by weak sales.

With little reason for a pick-up in Asia -- Christmas is superceded in most of the region by the paramount Lunar New Year holiday in early February -- dealers were pessimistic the pace would change before early January.

"There's no significant demand for gold in my business. This is the worst year we have experienced in the past 15 years," the Singapore jeweller said. "I hope it will pick up as we get nearer Christmas, but I'm not optimistic."
A dealer in Hong Kong said business activity should be noticeably better once the Christmas and New Year season has passed and buying for Lunar New Year kicks in.
The only bright spot he saw in the precious metals arena was palladium, which had picked up $2-3 this week to $119 an ounce, he said.

Quoting industry figures that put total 1996 demand at 6.1 million ounces, he said Russia held the card on palladium prices because the its exports had been higher than production for the past few years.
"Their oversupply has been putting a lid on palladium in the last couple of years," he said. "But if the Russians back away there will be a major readjustment in prices."
Russian supply contracts were due to be re-negotiated in January and February, he said.
With palladium demand mostly in the automotive, dental and electronic industries, genuine fundamentals were mostly behind price flows, he said.
-- Lynne O'Donnell in Hong Kong (852) 2843-6470
-- Rene Pastor in Singapore (65) 870-3174
